beats.intro: Chapter three, lesson one. Protein folding, and the bonds that hold it. [[yarn]]Here is a long strand of yarn, straight from the shop. [[ball]]And here it is, rolled into a ball. Same strand, very different shape, and the ball is the one that fits in the basket. A protein chain is a little like that. [[strip]]In this chapter we follow a protein from a loose chain to a working machine, in four levels: primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary. [[bonds]]Today we build that map, and then we meet the five bonds and forces that hold it together.
beats.fold: [[chain]]You met the chain in chapter two: amino acids joined by peptide links, with a free amino end, the N-terminal, and a free carboxyl end, the C-terminal. [[fold]]But a freshly made chain is not yet a working protein. Protein folding is the process by which a polypeptide chain folds into its biologically active shape, called the native three-dimensional structure. [[fn]]Shape matters, because the structure of a protein is crucial to its function. A folded protein has a pocket that fits its partner. Unfold it, or fold it wrongly, and the partner no longer fits. [[seq]]And different sequences of amino acids fold into different shapes. Every side chain is a different brick, and the order of the bricks decides where the chain bends.
beats.levels: [[l1]]The first level, primary structure, is the chain itself: the order of its amino acids. [[l2]]Secondary structure is the chain coiled or pleated into helices and sheets. [[l3]]Tertiary structure is those pieces folded into one compact three-dimensional shape. [[l4]]And quaternary structure is several folded chains packed together. The next two lessons take each level in turn. [[forces]]So what holds it all together? Folded proteins are held together by various bonds and forces. Two are covalent, and strong. Three are non-covalent, and weak.
beats.peptide: [[pep]]Strong bond number one: the peptide bond. [[join]]The carboxyl group of one amino acid meets the amino group of the next. [[water]]One molecule of water is removed, and what is left is the peptide link, a carbonyl group joined to an N H group, in orange. [[keep]]This is the bond that builds the chain itself, the primary structure. It is strong, and ordinary folding never breaks it.
beats.disulfide: [[cys]]Strong bond number two: the disulfide bridge. Cysteine is the amino acid with a sulfur in its side chain, in a sulfhydryl group. [[near]]When folding brings two cysteines side by side, [[ss]]each one gives up a hydrogen, two hydrogen atoms in all, and the two sulfurs join in a disulfide bridge. [[cystine]]Two cysteines joined like this make cystine, which you met in chapter one. [[brace]]The bridge works like a staple, clamping two faraway parts of the chain together.
beats.q1: Quick check. Two cysteine side chains lose two hydrogens and join. What bond forms?
beats.hbond: [[bb]]Now the weak bonds. First, hydrogen bonds. Along the backbone, every peptide link has a carbonyl oxygen and an N H group. [[hb]]A hydrogen bond forms between the carbonyl of one peptide link and the N H of another one nearby. [[delta]]Why do they attract? The oxygen is slightly negative, and the hydrogen slightly positive. Only slightly, so each single bond is weak. [[many]]But a chain makes a great many of them, and side chains can make them too. They are what holds the helices and sheets of the next lesson.
beats.salt: [[lys]]Next, salt bridges, also called electrostatic or ionic interactions. They form between oppositely charged side groups. Remember the charged amino acids from chapter one. Lysine is basic, and carries a positive charge. [[glu]]Glutamic acid is acidic, and carries a negative charge. [[pair]]When folding brings them close, plus meets minus, and they attract. [[both]]That close pair can also share a hydrogen, so some books draw the same pair as a hydrogen bond. It is one pair, not a new kind of bond.
beats.hydro: [[nonp]]Last, hydrophobic interactions. Some side chains are non-polar, like valine, leucine and isoleucine, and the ring of phenylalanine. They have no charge to offer the water around them. [[push]]Water crowds them out, so as the chain folds, [[gather]]they gather together in the core, and the polar and charged side chains stay outside, in the water. [[notbond]]The slide says no true bonds exist here. It is a tendency, not a link, but it is a big reason proteins keep their shape. Some books also mention van der Waals forces: tiny attractions between side chains packed close together, which is a different thing.
beats.q2: Quick check. Valine and leucine are non-polar. Where do they end up in a folded protein?
beats.together: [[all]]Let's put it together. [[glob]]Here is one folded chain. The peptide bonds and disulfide bridges are covalent, and strong. [[weak]]Hydrogen bonds, salt bridges and the hydrophobic core are each weak. But a protein makes very many of them, and together they hold the shape firmly, yet gently enough for the protein to do its work. [[side]]And look who acts most of them out: the side chains. Each bond happens between particular side chains, which is why the sequence decides the shape.
beats.wrap: To sum up. [[s1]]A polypeptide chain folds into its native shape, and the shape decides the function. [[s2]]There are four levels: primary, secondary, tertiary and quaternary. [[s3]]Two strong, covalent bonds: the peptide bond and the disulfide bridge. [[s4]]Three weak ones: hydrogen bonds, salt bridges and hydrophobic interactions. [[end]]Now try the practice.
